content_html:
Tax-loss harvesting means selling an investment that is worth less than you paid so the loss can cancel out taxable gains, and up to $3,000 of ordinary income, on your federal return. This calculator estimates what harvesting one losing position would save for the 2026 tax year. It works out your federal tax twice, once without the sale and once with it, using the 2026 brackets and capital gains rates, so the answer reflects how the loss actually flows through your return.

How to use this calculator

  1. Cost basis and current value: what you paid for the position, including fees, and what it would sell for now. The difference is the loss you would harvest.
  2. Held for: one year or less makes it a short-term loss; more than one year makes it long-term. The holding period starts the day after you bought.
  3. Planned sale date: used to show the wash sale window.
  4. Filing status and taxable income: your taxable income after deductions, leaving out capital gains, sets the rates your gains and income are taxed at.
  5. Other gains this year: net short-term and long-term gains you have already realized or expect, including capital gain distributions from funds.
  6. More options: loss carryovers from earlier years, a flat state income tax rate, trading costs and the 3.8% net investment income tax.

How the loss is applied

The IRS nets gains and losses in a set order, which this calculator follows:

  1. Short-term losses are netted against short-term gains, and long-term losses against long-term gains.
  2. If one group ends with a net loss, it offsets the net gain in the other group.
  3. If the overall result is a net loss, up to $3,000 ($1,500 if married filing separately) is deducted from ordinary income.
  4. Anything left over carries forward to future years with no time limit, keeping its short-term or long-term character.

A loss is worth the most when it cancels short-term gains or ordinary income, which are taxed at your regular rate of up to 37%. Against long-term gains it saves 0%, 15% or 20%, depending on your income.

Worked example

A single filer has $90,000 of taxable income before gains, $2,000 of short-term gains and $3,000 of long-term gains, and sells a stock bought eight months ago for $20,000 that is now worth $12,000. The $8,000 short-term loss first wipes out the $2,000 short-term gain, then the remaining $6,000 cancels the $3,000 long-term gain, and the final $3,000 is deducted from ordinary income. In the 22% bracket, that saves $2,000 × 22% + $3,000 × 15% + $3,000 × 22% = $1,550 of federal tax, from $15,402 down to $13,852. With a 5% state tax, about $400 more is saved, $1,950 in total.

The wash sale rule

If you buy the same security, or one that is substantially identical, within 30 days before or after the sale, the loss is disallowed for now and added to the basis of the new shares instead. That 61-day window also covers purchases in IRAs and a spouse's accounts, and automatic dividend reinvestment. Many investors stay invested by buying a fund that tracks a different index during the window, then switch back after it closes.

Limits of this estimate

  • It ignores tax credits, the alternative minimum tax, deduction phase-outs that depend on income, and the special 25% and 28% rates on some real estate and collectibles gains.
  • State tax is a flat-rate approximation. Some states tax capital gains differently or do not follow the federal loss rules.
  • Harvesting lowers your cost basis in the replacement holding, so part of the saving can come back as a larger gain when you sell later. The benefit is largest when the gain is deferred for a long time or never taxed.
  • Tax rules change, and this is an estimate, not tax advice. A tax professional can confirm your numbers.

faq.question: How much capital loss can I deduct in 2026?
faq.answer: Capital losses first offset capital gains without limit. If losses exceed gains, up to $3,000 of the net loss can be deducted from other income, or $1,500 if you are married filing separately. The rest carries forward to later years.

faq.question: Do unused capital losses expire?
faq.answer: For individuals, no. A net capital loss carries forward year after year until it is used, keeping its short-term or long-term character. It does not pass to heirs, however, so losses unused at death are lost.

faq.question: Is a short-term or long-term loss more valuable?
faq.answer: Neither is worth more in itself. What matters is what the loss ends up offsetting. A loss that cancels short-term gains or ordinary income saves tax at your regular rate, while one that cancels long-term gains saves at 0%, 15% or 20%. The netting rules decide which gains each loss offsets first.

faq.question: Can I harvest losses in a retirement account?
faq.answer: No. Gains and losses inside IRAs, 401(k)s and similar accounts are not reported each year, so selling at a loss there has no tax effect. Buying the same security in an IRA within the wash sale window can also permanently disallow a loss harvested in a taxable account.

faq.question: When is the deadline for tax-loss harvesting?
faq.answer: The sale must take place by the last trading day of the year to count for that tax year. Settlement can happen in January; the trade date is what matters for losses.

faq.question: Is my information stored or sent anywhere?
faq.answer: No. The calculation runs entirely in your browser, and nothing you enter is sent to a server or saved.
